CS10-05.note: No sentence states the purpose; it must be built from three clues (graded gravel/coarse sand under the topsoil, workable 2 days after a storm vs a week on the unterraced slope, maize up a fortnight earlier) plus the closing cost line that marks the gravel as deliberate, not incidental. B is the nearest rival and is actively contradicted: fast drying is the opposite of storing water for dry months. A is excluded by the text's own concession structure (erosion control 'asks only for a wall and packed earth'), C by the total absence of any freeze/heave cue. On the repairer's flag: I AGREE the warming half rests on one cue, and I agree that cue is formally ambiguous - earlier emergence is equally consistent with 'you could work and sow the ground sooner', i.e. drainage alone. I would put the key's support nearer 3/4 than full, as they say. It does not create a second defensible answer, because no other option names warming at all and the two halves are causally the same fact (a drained bed warms sooner). Risk here is not a wrong key but a solver who picks D on drainage alone and never tests the second half.

CS10-12.note: Text 2's rebuttal is assembled, not stated: a written instrument is cited by date and seal; it survives in NEITHER firm's archive; in 1438 both houses sent to ONE AND THE SAME chest. 'Third party' is the only reading that reconciles those three, so A. C is the designed trap and the one worth checking - 'ledgers each firm kept privately' fails on both 'the same chest' (one shared location, not two) and 'neither archive'. B and D are the position Text 1 already holds (trust/custom, nothing written) and are refused by the instrument's existence. Not second-defensible. An unusually generous reader could argue the chest belonged to one of the two houses rather than an outsider, but that still contradicts 'either firm's archive', and no option offers it.

CS10-17.note: Text 2 argues the air is depleted by what it already dropped crossing the front, so the ratio tracks the path the air took, not the ground under it - 'how far inland the air carrying the rain had traveled' is that, and the low modern basins returning high-terrain ratios is the confirming case. On the repairer's flag: the rainfall-amount distractor (A) is TEMPTING, NOT DEFENSIBLE, and I dispute nothing about the key. The amount effect is real and A will pull isotope-literate solvers, but A locates the rainfall in the wrong place and time - 'in the seasons when the leaves grew', i.e. local rain at the basin - whereas Text 2's whole mechanism is upwind rainout before the air ever arrives. Text 2 also says the stripping happens 'whatever the ground beneath it is doing', which explicitly rules out reading the ratio as a record of conditions at the fossil site. That clause is what keeps A out, and it is doing more work after the repair than before; I would not remove it. B (temperature) is the same species of trap and equally real-but-unclaimed, which is also why I still score passage_needed true: a knowledge-only solver has at least three genuine isotope controls to choose among and no basis to prefer one, so background knowledge does not select the key - it only narrows to A/B/C.
